title.en: Chuseok: Songpyeon and the Full Moon

summaryEn: At Chuseok (Hangawi), Hoya joins a family going back to their hometown, makes songpyeon steamed on pine needles, and watches women dance Ganggangsullae hand in hand under the full moon.
learningGoalsEn: Know when Chuseok falls (15th day of the 8th lunar month) and that its native name is Hangawi.
Understand what songpyeon are and how they are made (fillings; steamed on pine needles).
Understand Ganggangsullae (women in a circle, call-and-response singing) and know that UNESCO inscribed it in 2009.
Read and recognize 추석 (chuseok), 한가위 (hangawi), 송편 (songpyeon), 보름달 (boreumdal) and 강강술래 (ganggangsullae).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

keywords.ko: 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라
keywords.romanization: Deodo malgo deoldo malgo hangawiman gatara

scenes.narrationEn: It's {kw:chuseok}, also called Hangawi! It falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, just as the harvest begins. Families give thanks for the year's crops.
scenes.artBrief: Golden rice fields under an autumn sky, persimmon trees heavy with orange fruit; Hoya stretching happily at the edge of the field.

scenes.narrationEn: Many people travel back to their hometowns, {kw:gohyang}. In the morning, families honor their ancestors with a table of food, called charye, and then visit their ancestors' graves, called seongmyo.
scenes.captionEn: Charye and a visit to ancestors' graves
scenes.artBrief: A family in hanbok standing respectfully before a low table set with fruit and dishes; later a grassy hillside path; Hoya walking quietly with them.

scenes.narrationEn: On the night before Chuseok, under the bright moon, {kw:dal}, the family makes songpyeon together. They wrap rice dough around fillings like sesame, beans or chestnuts. Rice from the new harvest makes them extra tasty!

keyword.en: small filled rice cakes for Chuseok

scenes.artBrief: Family members around a low table shaping small white, green and pink rice cakes; bowls of sesame, beans and chestnuts; Hoya pinching one closed.

scenes.narrationEn: Many songpyeon are shaped like little half-moons. They are steamed on a bed of pine needles. Mmm, smell the fresh pine! Hoya tries one. Yum!
scenes.artBrief: A bamboo steamer opened to reveal glossy rice cakes resting on green pine needles, wisps of steam; Hoya sniffing with closed eyes.

scenes.narrationEn: On Chuseok night, a big round full moon rises. In old farming villages the full moon meant plenty, and Chuseok was even called 'the holiday of the moon.'
scenes.captionEn: A big round full moon rises
scenes.artBrief: A huge glowing full moon rising over a quiet village of thatched and tiled roofs; Hoya sitting on a stone wall gazing up.

scenes.narrationEn: Under the moon, women join hands in a circle for Ganggangsullae. A lead singer calls out a line, and everyone answers, 'Ganggangsullae!' The song starts slow, then gets faster and faster until they are almost running.
scenes.artBrief: Women in hanbok holding hands in a wide circle on a moonlit field, skirts swirling, one singer at the front; Hoya clapping along outside the circle.

scenes.narrationEn: Between dances they play games with fun names, like 'fern picking' and 'fish tying.' The dance has long been done along Korea's southwestern coast. And no one knows exactly what the word 'ganggangsullae' means!
scenes.artBrief: Dancers crouched in a line like ferns while a leader 'picks' them one by one; a coastline with small islands in the moonlight behind; Hoya scratching his head curiously.

scenes.narrationEn: In 2009, UNESCO added Ganggangsullae to its heritage list. The Joseon-era book Yeoryang sesigi records an old saying like this: 'No more, no less, may it always be like Hangawi!'
scenes.captionEn: UNESCO's list and an old Hangawi saying

facts.claimKo: 추석에는 많은 사람이 고향을 찾으며, 차례와 성묘가 추석의 대표 의례이다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 추석
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘Ancestral rites at home (charye) and at the graveyard (seongmyo) are the two definitive customs of Chuseok.’ / ‘many Koreans still return to their hometowns on Chuseok’

sources.title: 추석
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘추석날 아침 일찍 일어나 첫 번째 일은 차례를 지내는 일이다.’ / ‘아침식사를 마치고 조상의 산소에 가서 성묘를 하는데’

facts.claimEn: On the evening before Chuseok (the 14th), families gather under the bright moon to make songpyeon, rice-dough cakes filled with fillings such as beans, sesame or chestnuts; made from newly harvested grain, they taste especially good.
facts.claimKo: 추석 전날(열나흗날) 저녁 밝은 달을 보며 가족이 모여 콩·깨·밤 등을 소로 넣은 송편을 빚으며, 햇곡식으로 만들어 더욱 맛이 있다.

sources.title: 추석
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘열 나흗날 저녁 밝은 달을 보면서 가족들이 모여 송편을 만든다.’ / ‘송편 속에도 콩 · 팥 · 밤 · 대추 등을 넣는데, 모두 햇것으로 한다. 모두 햇곡식이기 때문에 더욱 맛이 있다.’

sources.title: 송편

facts.claimEn: Songpyeon are often shaped like a half-moon and are steamed on a layer of pine needles; the scent of pine is said to make the rice cake taste better.
facts.claimKo: 송편은 흔히 반달 모양으로 빚어 솔잎을 깔고 찌며, 솔잎의 소나무 향이 떡의 맛을 좋게 한다고 한다.

sources.title: 송편
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 어린이민속사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘송편은 멥쌀가루 반죽에 팥, 콩, 밤, 대추, 깨 등을 넣고 반달이나 모시조개 모양으로 만들어서 솔잎을 깔고 찐 떡입니다. … 솔잎에서 나오는 소나무 향은 떡의 맛을 좋게 합니다.’

sources.title: 송편 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘멥쌀가루를 익반죽하고 풋콩, 깨, 밤 같은 소를 넣어 반달 모양으로 빚어서 시루에 솔잎을 켜켜로 놓고 찐 떡.’

sources.title: 송편 (미디어 설명)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 미디어 캡션: ‘멥쌀가루를 뜨거운 물로 반죽하여 소를 넣고 모양을 만들어 솔잎을 깔고 찐 떡이다. 추석에 먹는 음식이다.’

facts.claimEn: In traditional farming life the Chuseok full moon was a symbol of plenty, and Chuseok was even called 'the holiday of the moon'.
facts.claimKo: 전통 농경사회에서 추석 보름달은 풍요를 상징했으며, 추석을 ‘달의 명절’이라 부르기도 했다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 추석
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘The full moon on Chuseok is understood as a symbol of prosperity, fecundity, and a bountiful crop.’ / ‘추석을 ‘달의 명절’이라 이르기도 하였다.’

facts.claimEn: In Ganggangsullae, performed on moonlit nights around Chuseok, women join hands and move in a circle; a lead singer sings a line and the others answer 'Ganggangsullae', and the song and dance start slow and grow faster until the dancers are almost running.
facts.claimKo: 강강술래는 추석 무렵 달밤에 여인들이 손에 손을 잡고 원을 그리며, 앞소리꾼이 메기면 나머지가 ‘강강술래’로 받는다. 처음엔 느리다가 점점 빨라져 나중에는 뛰는 듯하다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 강강술래 (Ganggangsullae)
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘여인들은 손에 손을 잡고 오른쪽으로 돌며 둥근 원을 그려나간다. 목청 좋고 소리 잘하는 사람이 맨 앞에 서서 메기는 소리를 하면 나머지 사람들은 ‘강강술래’하며 받는 소리를 한다. 처음에는 늦은 가락으로 나아가다 … 나중에는 뛰는 것처럼 동작이 빨라진다.’

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘Under a bright full moon, dozens of young, unmarried village women gather in a circle, join hands’ / ‘sing and dance all night under the direction of a lead singer.’

sources.title: 강강술래 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘동산에 보름달이 떠오르면 마을의 넓은 마당으로 모인 여자들이 느린 가락에 맞춰 늦은강강술래를 추다가 흥이 점점 더해감에 따라 속도가 빨라져서 마침내 잦은강강술래로 이어진다.’ / ‘한 사람이 설소리(앞소리)를 하면, 나머지 사람이 매김소리(뒷소리)를 받는’

facts.claimEn: Ganggangsullae includes accompanying folk games such as 'bracken picking' (gosari-kkeokgi) and 'herring tying' (cheongeo-yeokgi).
facts.claimKo: 강강술래에는 고사리꺾기, 청어엮기 등의 놀이가 곁들여진다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 강강술래
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘남생이놀이를 비롯해서 고사리꺾기, 청어엮기, 기와밟기, 꼬리따기 …’ / English: ‘folk games such as “bracken picking,” “herring tying,” “tile treading,”’

sources.title: 고사리타령
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘고사리꺾기 놀이는 강강술래 여흥 놀이의 하나로도 포함되어 있으나 독립적인 놀이로도 행해졌다.’

sources.title: 강강술래 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘남생이놀이, 고사리꺾기, 청어엮기, 지와밟기, 꼬리따기, 덕석말이 … 같은 여성들이 하는 놀이’

facts.claimEn: Ganggangsullae has traditionally been performed mainly along the southwestern coast of Korea (the coast of Jeollanam-do). Its exact origin is uncertain; the Korea Heritage Service considers an origin in ancient moonlit-night festivals more plausible than the popular Admiral Yi Sun-sin story.
facts.claimKo: 강강술래는 전통적으로 주로 한반도 서남 해안 지방(전라남도 해안)에서 행해졌다. 정확한 기원은 확실하지 않으며, 국가유산청은 이순신 장군 유래설보다 달 밝은 밤의 고대 축제에서 비롯되었다고 보는 것이 타당하다고 설명한다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 강강술래
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘주로 전라남도 해안지방에서 추석을 전후하여 달밤에 행해졌다.’ / ‘임진왜란 때 이순신 장군이 … 비롯되었다는 설이 있으나, 원시시대부터 1년중 가장 달이 밝은 밤에 축제를 벌여 노래하고 춤추던 풍습에서 비롯된 민속놀이라고 보는 것이 타당하다.’

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘a seasonal harvest and fertility ritual popular in the south-western part of the Republic of Korea’

sources.title: 강강술래
sources.quoteOrLocator: 정의: ‘추석날 밤이나 정월 대보름날 밤에 … 서남 해안지방에서 행하는 노래와 무용과 놀이가 혼합된 성인여자놀이.’

sources.title: 강강술래 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘강강술래의 유래는 확실하지 않다.’ / ‘전승 지역으로 보면 호남 일원이요, 연행 시기로 보면 8월 한가위가 일반적이며, 연행 주체는 주로 마을의 여자들이다.’

facts.claimEn: The dance is named after its refrain, but the exact meaning of the word 'ganggangsullae' is unknown.
facts.claimKo: 강강술래라는 이름은 후렴에서 왔지만 그 말의 정확한 뜻은 알려져 있지 않다.

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘The dance takes its name from the refrain repeated after each verse, although the exact meaning of the word is unknown.’

facts.claimEn: Ganggangsullae was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009.

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘Inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity’

facts.claimEn: The Joseon-era book Yeoryang sesigi (by Gim Mae-sun) records people saying, in Chinese characters, 'No more, no less, may it always be like Hangawi'; the familiar modern Korean wording is 'Deodo malgo deoldo malgo hangawiman gatara'.
facts.claimKo: 조선시대 김매순의 『열양세시기(洌陽歲時記)』에는 ‘더도 말고 덜도 말고 늘 한가위 같기만 바란다’는 뜻의 말이 한자로 실려 있으며, 오늘날 널리 쓰이는 표현은 “더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라”이다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 추석
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘조선시대 『열양세시기(冽陽歲時記)』에는 4대 명절이었던 추석을 중히 여겨 … 이런 의미로 “더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라”는 말이 수록되어 있다.’ (KHS gives the modern wording; the Hanja form is in the Folk Encyclopedia entry below)

sources.title: 더도 말고 덜도 말고 늘 가윗날만 같아라 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘김매순(金邁淳)의 『열양세시기(冽陽歲時記)』 8월 중추(中秋)에 보면 … 그래서 말하기를 ‘더도 말고 덜도 말고 늘 한가위 같기만 바란다(加也勿 減夜勿 但願長似嘉俳日)’라고 한다.’라고 기록되어 있다.’ (the dictionary prints 減夜勿)

sources.title: 열양세시기 (한국민속예술사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: ‘조선 순조 때 김매순이 열양, 즉 한양의 연중행사를 편찬한 세시 풍속 자료집.’ / ‘1819년 기묘년 유두일에 열양외사가 썼다는 기문에 서울의 풍속 80여 가지를 수록하였다’

verification.notes: Third independent pass over 6 episodes / 61 facts / 161 source entries (70 unique URLs). Every URL was re-fetched with my own scripts (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies; heritage.go.kr descriptions via the portal ajax html and khs.go.kr open API; folkency via its JSON API) and each quote or locator was machine-matched to the page text; the few non-matching strings were checked by hand (portal metadata fields, hanja or footnote punctuation, label text). Corrections: (1) pansori scene 2 now gives both UNESCO steps (2003 masterpiece proclamation, 2008 Representative List); (2) pansori f11 states the Aesop title as in the cited Townsend text and the common alternate title; (3) added sources: NFM 놀보박타령 for 'greedy' (f5), 표준국어대사전 타다 for 'sawed' (f6), 한국민족문화대백과사전 선도해 for the Samguk sagi tale (f12); (4) Seollal f9/f10 designation-date locators now cite the KHS open API field. No other change. See seasons-tales.signoff.md.

authorNotes: Left out on purpose: the popular claim that Ganggangsullae began as Admiral Yi Sun-sin's military trick. The 국가유산포털 mentions it only as one theory and says an origin in ancient moonlit-night festivals is more plausible, so it isn't used. Also left out are folk etymologies of 'ganggangsullae' (UNESCO says the meaning is unknown), songpyeon fortune-telling beliefs (spouse looks, pregnancy divination), and specific 차례 table rules. Songpyeon shape symbolism (half-moon) isn't claimed because the sources don't support it. The 국가유산포털 actually links songpyeon to the full moon in general terms. The existing heritage-cards.ts text 'half-moon rice cakes' and 'steamed on pine needles for fragrance' is only partly supported: pine-needle steaming is supported, but the shape and fragrance claims weren't verified. UNESCO describes the original dancers as young unmarried village women; today mostly middle-aged women in cities keep it alive. The narration says 'women'. 'Tile treading' was skipped because explaining it (walking on bent backs) needs care for young children.
